siege

/SEEJ/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Siege means a military operation in which armed forces surround a fortified place and cut off its supplies to force surrender; figuratively, a prolonged period of relentless pressure.

The medieval army began its siege of the castle by blocking every road, so that not a single cart of grain could reach the defenders inside.

Example

After the scandal broke, the senator's office was under siege from reporters who camped outside the doors for a solid week.

No army is involved here — siege is being used figuratively. The reporters surrounded the office and kept up relentless, inescapable pressure, just as a besieging army surrounds a fortress.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

blockade: A blockade seals a place off so supplies cannot enter, and it can be run from a distance — warships closing a whole coastline. A siege is the fuller operation around one fortified place: surround it, starve it, force its surrender. The blockade is one tool; the siege is the whole strangling campaign.

encirclement: Encirclement names the maneuver of surrounding a place on all sides — the geometry of a moment, complete once the ring closes. A siege is what the ring then does for weeks or months: cutting supplies and grinding the defenders toward surrender. Encirclement draws the circle; the siege is the long squeeze that follows.

entrapment: Entrapment is trapping someone with no way to escape — any trap, anywhere, from a box canyon to a courtroom sting. A siege is one specific, formal version: an army enclosing a fortified place and strangling its supplies. All sieges entrap; very few traps rise to a siege.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

relief: the rescue of a surrounded place by breaking the enemy's grip

retreat: the withdrawal of forces away from a place

Where it sits · how actively force is applied — standoff → siege → onslaught

standoff vs. siege: In a standoff, two forces face each other and wait; in a siege, one force surrounds the other and slowly strangles its supplies.

onslaught vs. siege: A siege wears a stronghold down over weeks or months; an onslaught tries to overwhelm it all at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — siege

Root — siege: from Old French sege, "a seat," from Latin sedere, "to sit" — the word came into English whole

Put it together

Put it together: A siege is literally a "sitting": the attacking army sits down outside a city's walls and refuses to leave until hunger forces the defenders to surrender.

Use the root in a new word: sediment

Use the root in a new word: sediment: Layers of sediment settled at the bottom of the still, glassy lake.

Word Building

Word Choice

Neutral — history & news

Learn the two fixed phrases: an army lays siege to a city, and the city is then under siege. The figurative use is everywhere in modern news — a coach under siege from critics, a phone under siege from spam calls — always meaning relentless, surrounding pressure that will not let up.
